name: Cerberus Frost
geological_features: Three distinct ice caps of different chemical compositions at the poles and equator
Subsurface ocean detected between the equatorial ice and the rocky mantle
Ice quake zones where the three ice formations grind against each other
specific_features: A predator species that hunts across all three ice zones, adapted to metabolize different ice chemistries
Seismic patterns in the ice quake zones that follow a three-beat rhythm
description: Cerberus Frost is a world of three ices. Its surface is divided into distinct frozen domains: water ice at the north pole, carbon dioxide ice at the south, and ammonia ice in a broad equatorial band. The boundaries where these formations meet are zones of constant seismic activity, the different ice types grinding against each other with a violence that generates heat sufficient to maintain liquid pockets at the interfaces. The three-part division gives the planet a tricolor appearance from orbit, white and pale blue and amber.

The thin atmosphere carries ice crystals from all three formations, creating halos and atmospheric effects of unusual complexity. In the boundary zones, the air is thick with particulate ice and the crackling of static discharge as dissimilar crystals collide. The seismic activity follows a distinctive three-beat pattern that has been attributed to resonance between the ice masses, each one vibrating at its own frequency and the boundaries amplifying the combined signal into a planetary drumbeat felt through the ground.

The predator species that hunts across all three ice zones is Cerberus Frost's biological wonder. Evolved to metabolize different ice chemistries depending on their hunting ground, these three-headed organisms, or rather organisms with three distinct metabolic systems housed in a single body, range across the entire surface in pursuit of the smaller organisms that live in each ice type. Their population has been declining as the equatorial ammonia ice slowly sublimates, shrinking their territory.

The subsurface ocean beneath the equatorial ice represents the planet's primary strategic resource, containing deuterium concentrations that make it valuable as fusion fuel feedstock. Accessing the ocean requires drilling through the ammonia ice, which poses environmental risks to both the ice formation and the organisms that depend on it. Conservation advocates argue that the three-ice ecosystem is unique and irreplaceable, while energy interests note that the deuterium reserves could power a sector for generations. The three-beat seismic rhythm continues underneath the debate, indifferent to its outcome.
